$comment: Owner-declared scopes for claims the real corpus corroborates. A scope says what a claim was actually tested within. It is a property of the claim, not of the document that asserted it, which is why two independent sources can share one and corroborate each other. It is never inferred: extraction has no way to know a sentence's tested boundary, and guessing one would be the same self-certification this replaces.
$howToUse: Run the Learning cycle proof once with this list empty. It stops without promoting anything and reports every claim the real corpus asserts through two or more independently identified sources. Pick one, add a declaration for it below with an experiment that genuinely tests it and a verifier with a distinct identity, and run again. A declaration needs claim, claimScope, and generalizationBoundary. The claim is matched against what the corpus corroborates by the deterministic same-meaning test in src/semanticCorroboration.js, which accepts paraphrase but never crosses a negation or a changed number.
$boundaries: A declaration authorizes evaluation, never promotion, and this is true of a pairing too. Nominating two sources decides which claim gets tested; it never decides whether the claim is true. The controlled experiment still has to pass, the critical reviewer still rejects ambiguous wording before any testing, a distinct independent verifier still has to agree, and a failed control still blocks the claim regardless of what is declared here.

declarations.claim: For example, the Array object's map function allows you to iterate over each element of an array, then build a new array by applying a transform function to each element.
declarations.claimScope: Node.js ordinary dense arrays of numbers
declarations.generalizationBoundary: Does not cover sparse arrays, proxies, subclasses, or host objects.
pairedAssertions: For example, the Array object's map function allows you to iterate over each element of an array, then build a new array by applying a transform function to each element.
See full compatibility Learn more The map() method of Array instances creates a new array populated with the results of calling a provided function on every element in the calling array.

declarations.claim: Any class can have more than one constructor.
declarations.claimScope: Java classes compiled and executed by OpenJDK 21, whose constructors differ in parameter list
declarations.generalizationBoundary: Does not cover other JDK versions, other JVM languages, records, enums or interfaces, or constructors distinguished by anything other than parameter list.
declarations.$whyNoPairing: pairedSources is deliberately absent. The corpus own semantic test already related the two asserting sentences at the configured 0.74 threshold - "Any class can have more than one constructor." from linked-source:28503d6f107c6d879b9a251ad0c10598865e2d6aeeec816f8431dae855b8068e and "The class can also include one or more constructors." from owner-file:7a409be17956fa11e90c634d6de5a586d0415d668c56d252f66fb5580a362d9b. $ownerPairing exists for wording too different for that test to relate; nominating a pairing here would substitute owner judgement for the machine where the machine succeeded.

$ownerPairing: When two sources agree in wording too different for that test to relate - one says "does not modify the original" and the other says "leaves the input untouched" - add pairedSources with exactly the two source ids, and pairedAssertions with the sentence each of those documents uses, in the same order. Each sentence must appear verbatim among that document's own bounded assertions, and the corpus is checked against the hash the queue recorded, so a pairing can never make a document say something it does not say. Sameness of meaning is then recorded as your judgement, not the machine's: the comparison decision carries agreementBasis "owner-declared". Omit pairedAssertions to have the wording test locate the asserting sentence itself.
$preRegistration: A declaration is the hypothesis, so it is pre-registered like one. Nothing here writes a hypothesis by hand: src/languageExperimentRegistry.js builds it as "Within <boundary>, controlled execution will show that <claim>", and src/hypothesisTestPlan.js then holds the experiment to the declared claimScope. Every falsifiable commitment therefore comes from this file. The first run to see a declaration records the SHA-256 of its claim, claimScope, generalizationBoundary, language, pairedSources and pairedAssertions against that run own clock, in scope-pre-registration.json beside the learning store. Later runs compare. Commentary and whitespace are excluded from the hash, so rewording a note or reflowing a long boundary is not a change. There is deliberately no declaredAt field to fill in: a timestamp typed here could be backdated with a text editor, and a field that looks like evidence without being evidence is worse than none. What cannot be forged from this file is that a run saw a hash and wrote it down.
$whenTheBoundaryMayChange: Picking which claim to test from what the corpus corroborates is legitimate, and the $boundaries note below says why: nominating sources decides what gets tested, never whether it is true. The boundary is the part that cannot move freely, because it is where the degrees of freedom are - a scope narrowed far enough cannot be falsified by anything. So: a declaration no experiment has run on yet may be corrected freely, which is what keeps an unpairable declaration fixable. A declaration whose claim was already verified may be re-declared, because the knowledge version keeps the boundary it was actually verified at and a different boundary is a new experiment; the prior registration is kept in history rather than overwritten. A declaration that changed after a controlled experiment on that same claim ran and did not verify it is refused with CRU-0047, because after the fact that cannot be told apart from narrowing the boundary until the claim stopped failing. If the new boundary is a genuinely different question, declare it as a different claim so it pre-registers and is tested on its own. If the pre-registered boundary was simply wrong, the honest record is that the claim failed within the boundary it was declared for.
